prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

For James Welch The first harvest of wheat in flatlands along the Milk startled me into thoughts of you and this place we both remember and also forget as home. Maybe it was the familiarity or maybe it was my own need to ask if you have ever regretted leaving. What bends, what gives? And have you ever missed this wind?—it has now grown warm with late summer, but soon it will be as dangerous as the bobcat stalking calves and pets just south of the river. Men take out their dogs, a case of beer and wait in their pickups for dawn, for a chance with their rifles. They don’t understand that she isn’t going to make any mistakes. With winter my need for an answer grows more desperate and there are only four roads out. One is the same cat hunters drive with mannish glory and return along, gun still oil-shined and unshot. Another goes deeper into Assiniboine territory: This is the one I should talk myself into taking next. I haven’t much traveled the third except to visit a hospital where, after the first time, my mother had refused chemotherapy. And the last road you know as well as I do— past the coral-painted Catholic church, its doors long ago sealed shut to the mouth of Mission Canyon, then south just a ways, to where the Rockies cut open and forgive. There you and I are on the ascent. After that, the arrival is what matters most.

**For James Welch**

The first wheat harvest in the flatlands along the Milk startled me into thoughts of you and this place we both remember—and forget—as home. Maybe it was the familiarity, or maybe it was my own need to ask whether you have ever regretted leaving. What bends, what gives? And have you ever missed this wind? outputs.L2:
**To James Welch**

Seeing wheat gathered for the first time from the level country beside the Milk brought you suddenly to mind, along with this place we alternately claim and lose as home. Perhaps recognition stirred me; perhaps I simply needed to know whether you have ever been sorry you left. What yields, and what breaks? Do you ever long for this wind? Late summer has warmed it now, though before long it will turn as threatening as the female bobcat hunting calves and household animals south of the river. Men bring their dogs and a case of beer, then sit in their trucks until sunrise, rifles ready for an opportunity. They fail to realize that the cat will give them none.

As winter approaches, my desire for an answer becomes urgent. Only four roads lead away. One is the route taken by the bobcat hunters, who set out full of masculine pride and come back the same way, their guns still gleaming with oil and never fired. A second carries on farther into Assiniboine land; next time, I ought to persuade myself to choose it. I have rarely followed the third road, except when going to the hospital where my mother, after her first treatment, declined any more chemotherapy. The fourth is as familiar to you as it is to me: it passes the Catholic church painted coral, whose doors were sealed years ago, continues to the entrance of Mission Canyon, and then runs a short distance south to the place where the Rockies split apart and offer absolution. There, you and I are climbing. Beyond that point, reaching the destination is what matters above all.
outputs.L3:
The first wheat harvest along the Milk River awakens the speaker’s memories of James Welch and of the place they once shared—a home that has become distant and partly forgotten. The familiar landscape prompts the speaker to wonder whether Welch ever regretted leaving or still missed the region’s relentless wind. For now, that wind remains part of the open country, but winter is approaching, and it will soon become harsh enough to threaten anyone caught unprepared.

Meanwhile, local men set out to hunt a bobcat that has been preying on calves and household pets. Although the community treats the animal as a danger that must be eliminated, the speaker believes it will escape. The bobcat’s ability to survive and remain beyond reach reflects the wildness of the landscape itself, as well as the persistence of things that cannot easily be captured, controlled, or understood.

As winter draws nearer, the speaker’s desire for answers becomes increasingly urgent. The four roads leading away from the area represent more than physical routes: each suggests a different history, memory, or possible future. The final road is one that both the speaker and Welch know well. It passes a sealed Catholic church and continues toward the Rocky Mountains. In that westward journey, the road becomes almost spiritual. To climb toward the mountains and finally arrive is to move beyond uncertainty and loss, reaching a place where reconciliation—and perhaps forgiveness—becomes possible.
outputs.L4:
Addressing James Welch as both companion and guide, the speaker reflects on the complicated pull of home. Memory shapes the journey, but it does not provide a clear or reliable map. Instead, the past appears through fragments: changing seasons, familiar landscapes, dangerous places, and roads that seem to promise a return while also leading farther away. Departure has created distance, yet that distance intensifies longing. Home remains powerful precisely because it can no longer be recovered in a simple or complete form.

The seasonal imagery underscores the passage of time and the emotional uncertainty of travel. Shifts in weather and light suggest that the landscape is never fixed; it changes just as memory changes. Places once known intimately may become strange, while forgotten details unexpectedly return. The local dangers along the way remind the travelers that Montana is not merely an idealized homeland. It is a real place marked by risk, hardship, history, and loss. To return to it requires more than nostalgia—it requires confronting what has happened there and acknowledging the wounds carried by both the land and its people.

The four roads through Montana offer different directions, but none guarantees an uncomplicated arrival. They represent possible routes through memory as much as physical paths across the state. Each road holds traces of experience, and each invites the travelers to reconsider what they believe they have left behind. As they move forward, remembered places blur with forgotten ones. Home becomes a paradox: it is the place they know most deeply and the place they may no longer fully recognize.

Yet the journey does not end in despair. The shared ascent toward the Rockies gives the movement a sense of purpose and renewal. Climbing together suggests that reconciliation is possible, even when the past cannot be restored. The mountains become a destination and a spiritual horizon, a place toward which grief, affection, and hope can be carried. In addressing Welch, the speaker also creates a bond between travelers, writers, and witnesses whose experiences of Montana overlap without being identical.

Ultimately, arrival matters not because it erases exile or repairs every loss, but because it affirms the continuing possibility of connection. Forgiveness may come through recognizing the limits of memory, accepting what has been forgotten, and continuing the journey despite uncertainty. Home is therefore more than a location. It is an enduring relationship to landscape, history, community, and the people with whom one travels. Even when home can only be approached through memory, the act of moving toward it remains meaningful.
outputs.L5:
### For James Welch

For James Welch, writing was a way to preserve memory, confront history, and portray the lives of Native American communities with honesty. Born in Montana in 1940, Welch drew upon his Blackfeet and A’aninin heritage to create poetry and fiction rooted in the landscapes of the American West.

Works such as *Winter in the Blood*, *Fools Crow*, and *The Heartsong of Charging Elk* explore identity, displacement, cultural survival, and belonging. Welch’s characters often face the lasting effects of colonialism while searching for purpose in a changing world.

James Welch helped bring Native American perspectives to a wider literary audience. His work remains valued for its vivid language, emotional depth, and enduring commitment to Indigenous history and experience.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem dedicated to James Welch, set along Montana’s Milk River, exploring memory, home, departure, grief, and the four roads leading out.
counterfactuals.output:
**Four Roads from the Milk River**  
*for James Welch*

At evening the Milk River carries the color of old tin, then ash, then the dark blue a bruise remembers after the body has healed. Cottonwoods lean over it as if listening for names. The wind comes down from Canada with dust in its mouth, worrying the grass, lifting the feathers of abandoned nests. Here, memory does not rise cleanly. It circles low, like a hawk over stubble, searching for what the years have left alive.

Home was never only the house with its porch listing east, nor the stove ticking through winter, nor the horses turning their black shoulders to the snow. Home was the long ache between distances: coulee and field, river and sky, the graveyard beyond the fence where stones kept their difficult silence. We belonged to what would not keep us. Even the river, called Milk, carried silt, fence wire, drowned light—everything mixed with leaving.

There are four roads leading out.

One goes north, where the cold enters early and the border is a line drawn across the wind. Along that road, a boy rides in the back of a truck, his hand raised until the house becomes a pale thumb in the mirror. He does not know departure has already begun to speak through him.

One goes south through wheat and heat-shimmer, past bars with dark windows and towns that close before sunset. A man follows it carrying the names of the dead like coins he cannot spend. At each crossing he hears laughter from another summer, though no one is there.

One road runs east beside the railroad, faithful to distance. The trains pass at night, their iron cry loosening every dream from its post. Grief travels that way: without turning, without apology, taking the last bright face beyond the reach of calling.

The fourth goes west into weather. Mountains gather far off, blue as withheld words. This is the road we imagine will return us changed, forgiven, able to enter the old rooms without waking their sorrow. But the road knows better. It bends, and bends again, until coming home and leaving are the same motion.

James, your words still walk these roads. They move through the grass where horses once stood, through snow that erases the tracks but not the going. They sit beside the river at dusk and listen to water carry what cannot be buried: a father’s voice, a mother’s hands, the door closing softly, the nation of the vanished and remembered.

Night settles over the Milk River. One by one, the roads disappear, though they remain beneath the dark, leading outward in every direction. The stars come on like small fires kept for travelers. Somewhere a meadowlark gives its last broken song.

And the river goes on, not toward forgetting, but through it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph piece of literary nonfiction in which the wheat harvest makes the narrator think of an absent friend and wonder whether they regret leaving home. Include a wary bobcat, unsuccessful hunters, a mother refusing chemotherapy, an abandoned Catholic church, and the Rockies.
counterfactuals.output: At wheat harvest, when the combines move through the fields like ships in a yellow sea and the chaff hangs bright as dust in the evening, I think of you in the city you chose beyond the Rockies, and wonder whether the smell of cut grain ever reaches you there, whether you regret leaving home. The men who spent October tracking elk came back unsuccessful, their coolers empty, their jokes thinned by hunger and pride; even the wary bobcat has begun appearing at the tree line, pausing to study the farmhouse as if it, too, suspects something is ending. Mother has refused chemotherapy, calmly, with the same voice she once used to turn down the beds, and now she sits by the window watching the stubble darken while I drive past the abandoned Catholic church, its white paint lifting in scales, the Virgin gone from her niche, swallows entering through the broken rose window. Beyond it, the Rockies hold the last light in their snowfields, beautiful and indifferent, and I imagine you looking back across them toward us, toward the empty pews and failed hunters, toward Mother and the bobcat and the harvest closing over another year, asking yourself—as I do—whether departure was courage, or only a distance that grew too wide to cross.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an evocative prose poem about northeastern Montana and the Assiniboine country, using late-summer wind, winter, rural roads, and mountain travel as metaphors for longing and loss?
counterfactuals.output:
**Roads Through the Buffalo Country**

By late August, the wind has learned every name we tried to forget. It moves through the wheat and silver sage, over the Milk River’s slow bends, worrying the grass until the whole prairie seems to lean toward something gone. In Assiniboine country, distance is not emptiness. It is a presence—old trails beneath the roads, old songs held close to the earth, the sky carrying more memory than any one heart can bear.

We drove north on a gravel road where the fence posts dwindled into heat, each mile a small leaving. Behind us, the farmhouses shut their white doors. Ahead, the horizon kept its promise by never arriving. You rested your hand near mine, not touching, while dust rose in the mirrors and made ghosts of everything we had passed.

Winter came early that year. Snow sealed the coulees, covered the two-tracks, softened the abandoned machinery into patient animals. At night the cold entered the walls and lay down beside us. Loss was like that: not a cry, but a weather; not a wound, but the long white field where no tracks return.

Later, alone, I crossed the mountains westward. The road climbed through lodgepole and stone, bent above rivers the color of iron. Every switchback offered the valley again, smaller and farther below, as if longing were a place seen repeatedly and never reached. At the pass, snow blew sideways in June. I thought of the northeastern plains, of wind combing the grass around Fort Peck, of the wide country holding what cannot be owned: bison shadow, river light, the quiet endurance of the Assiniboine people, whose homeland is not metaphor but living ground.

Then the descent—always the descent. Brakes warming, ears ringing, the road uncoiling toward another town. I carried your absence with me like prairie dust in the seams of a coat, like winter hidden in the high country, like a rural road after dark: one pale beam ahead, everything else immense, and the heart going on because there is nowhere to turn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a meditative letter addressed “For James Welch” that blends Indigenous Montana landscapes with memories of illness, religion, dangerous wildlife, and a shared journey toward the Rocky Mountains.
counterfactuals.output:
**For James Welch**

Dear James,

I write from the long grass east of the mountains, where the wind moves as if it remembers every name spoken here—Blackfeet names, Aaniiih names, names covered by survey maps but never wholly erased. The Sweet Grass Hills rise from the plains like old thoughts. Farther west, the Rocky Mountain Front gathers its blue weather around itself.

When I was ill, the hospital window held only a narrow strip of sky. Machines counted what my body could not: breath, pulse, the small distances between danger and sleep. A priest came carrying oil and a pocket Bible. He asked whether I wished to pray. I told him I had already been praying—to the cottonwoods along the Milk River, to the magpies quarreling beyond the glass, to my grandmother’s hands folding and unfolding a worn handkerchief. He nodded as though God might also travel by those roads.

You visited in memory, though we had not yet begun our journey. You stood at the foot of the bed with dust on your boots and said the mountains were waiting. Not kindly, not cruelly. Mountains do not wait as people do. They remain.

So we drove west beneath a sky immense enough to make belief feel both possible and foolish. The prairie towns passed: grain elevators, boarded churches, dogs asleep beside gas pumps. On the reservation roads, horses watched from behind wire. We spoke little. Illness had made every word expensive.

Near Two Medicine, a grizzly crossed ahead of us, dark-backed and deliberate. For one breath the road belonged entirely to danger. The bear turned its blunt head, and I felt the old fear rise—not only of teeth and muscle, but of being judged by something that had survived without asking permission. Then it vanished into the lodgepole shadows.

You laughed softly. “There,” you said, “is a sermon.”

By evening, snow had begun along the peaks. We stopped where the plains leaned upward into stone. Behind us lay the hospital, the chapel, the long country of fever. Before us, the Rockies held their white silence. I thought of baptism, of rivers, of all the ways people are told they can begin again. Yet the land seemed to say there is no beginning without what came before—no clean water without mud, no healing that does not carry its scar.

We walked until the light thinned. Above us, an eagle circled once and drifted toward the divide. I wanted to call it a sign, but you let it remain a bird.

That was your kindness.

Now, whenever sickness returns in the night, I remember the road bending toward the mountains and the bear entering the trees. I remember that fear can accompany us without becoming our guide. I remember your silence beside me, steady as the grass under snow.

The journey continues, James. The wind still crosses Montana, lifting dust from old trails. The mountains are ahead of us, and behind us, and within every mile we have survived.

Yours in the long light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary Western prose poem in a restrained, elegiac voice. Begin with the first wheat harvest along the Milk River, ask an old companion whether they miss home, describe four possible roads out, and end by emphasizing ascent and arrival.
counterfactuals.output: The first wheat harvest along the Milk River came in under a sky the color of an old tin cup. Combines moved through the fields after dusk, their lights wavering in the dust, and the grain trucks leaned hard into the rutted approaches. We were younger then, though not young, and believed the land kept what it took from us. Old friend, do you miss home—the pump coughing awake before dawn, the cottonwoods worrying the roof, the long blue weather gathering at the Canadian line? There were four roads out: east beside the river, where abandoned elevators stood like unmarked graves; west toward the mountains, pale as smoke above the stubble; south through the breaks, past cattle guards and towns reduced to a bar, a church, a blinking tower; north to the border, where the pavement narrowed and every name became another country. We tried them all in our minds. In the end, leaving was less a direction than a grade. The engine labored, the wheat fell away behind us, and mile by mile we climbed—out of the valley, into the thinning light—until the road crested and we arrived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
